passage:
Dear Deepika,

Thank you for the dal you left at my door last week. I didn't answer the bell. I'm sorry.

It's been four months since Ma died, and some days I still can't get out of bed. The office gave me leave, and I've gone back part-time. My desk feels strange. I keep picking up my phone to call her.

My counsellor suggested I make one small plan each day. Today it was a walk to the temple where she used to go. I sat there for an hour. It helped a little.

I'm going to try to come to your Sunday lunch. If I leave early, please don't take it badly. I just need people around who don't need me to be okay yet.

Manoj

qa.q: How long had it been since Manoj's mother died?
qa.a: It had been four months.

qa.q: Why didn't Manoj answer the bell when Deepika brought dal?
qa.a: Manoj was still deep in grief and didn't have the energy to see anyone that day.

qa.q: What is Manoj doing to rebuild a routine?
qa.a: Making one small plan each day, like a walk to the temple, and returning to work part-time with a counsellor's support.

qa.q: What might Deepika want to know from this letter?
qa.a: Deepika might want to know the help mattered and how best to be around Manoj without adding pressure.

grounding: Shows a young adult slowly rebuilding routine and support after Ma's death.

passage: The day they let me go, I went home at noon and sat on the bed in my office clothes till it got dark. Eighteen months at that company, and a ten-minute call ended it. My friend Mohit came over at nine with parathas. He didn't give advice. He just made me eat. The next week was the worst. I stopped shaving, stopped answering my parents. Mohit kept texting, small things, a meme, 'Zubin, you up?'. One morning he showed up and said we were going to the library. I made a list there: update CV, call two old colleagues, apply to three jobs a week. It took four months. What held me together was a routine, and one friend who didn't give up on me.

qa.q: How long had Zubin worked at the company?
qa.a: Zubin had worked there for eighteen months.

qa.q: What does sitting on the bed in office clothes till dark show about how Zubin felt?
qa.a: It shows Zubin was in shock and felt numb and lost after losing the job so suddenly.

qa.q: What helped Zubin start rebuilding?
qa.a: A simple routine with clear small goals, and a friend who kept checking in and pushing gently.

qa.q: What is it like for Mohit to support Zubin?
qa.a: He keeps showing up and staying patient even when Zubin withdraws, which takes steady care.

grounding: Shows a young adult rebuilding routine and support after sudden job loss.

passage: I'm Lalremsiami. Binita and I shared a room in the working women's hostel in Aizawl. Last year her fiancé was killed in a road accident. For weeks she barely spoke. She stopped going to her Sunday choir. I didn't know what to say, so I just brought her tea and sat with her. One evening she asked me to walk with her to choir practice. She stood at the back and didn't sing. The next week, she sang one hymn. Her supervisor let her start later in the mornings for a while. She started seeing a counsellor from the church. She still cries some nights. But she comes to choir every week now, and she's started laughing at the old ladies' jokes again.

qa.q: Where did Binita and Lalremsiami share a room?
qa.a: They shared a room in the working women's hostel in Aizawl.

qa.q: What might Binita standing at the back and not singing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt drawn back to her choir but was still too sad to join in fully.

qa.q: What supports helped Binita rebuild?
qa.a: Her roommate's quiet company, returning to choir step by step, a flexible start at work and seeing a counsellor.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami see their own role in Binita's recovery?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt unsure what to say, but that quiet company and tea were part of what helped. 🤍

grounding: Shows an observer watching a young woman slowly rebuild routine, support and meaning after grief.

passage: Week one: Chinmay was laid off on a Tuesday, along with half his team. For five days he slept past noon, stopped answering calls and ate cereal for dinner. When his younger brother Eshaan visited, the curtains were still closed at four. Week three: Eshaan came back with groceries and a proposal. 'Wake up by eight, walk with me, then two hours on applications. Just that.' Chinmay grumbled but agreed. He also called his old college mentor, which he had been too ashamed to do. The mentor listened, then sent him three contacts. Week eight: Chinmay had a routine: morning walk, applications, and an evening shift teaching coding at a community centre, unpaid but steadying. He still had bad days, when rejections hurt. But teaching gave him something the job hadn't: a reason to get up that was about other people. Two interviews were lined up.

qa.q: When was Chinmay laid off?
qa.a: On a Tuesday, along with half his team.

qa.q: Why had Chinmay avoided calling his college mentor?
qa.a: He felt too ashamed about losing his job.

qa.q: What helped Chinmay rebuild after the layoff?
qa.a: A simple routine, reaching out to his mentor, and teaching at a community centre, which gave him structure, support and meaning.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt seeing the curtains closed at four?
qa.a: Worried about his brother, which is why he came back with groceries and a gentle plan.

grounding: Shows a young man rebuilding routine, support and meaning over several weeks after losing his job.

passage: Payal, sit with your Vandana Aunty. When my husband died, I was twenty-six, with a two-year-old and a tailoring class I had just started. For weeks I didn't open the shop. I sat in his chair, holding his shirts. People told me to be strong. I hated that word. What helped was small. My neighbour came each morning at nine and said, 'Chai?' and we drank it without talking. After a month she said, 'The girls from the class keep asking.' I went back for one hour a day. Just one. Some days I cried over the sewing machine, and the girls pretended not to see and kept stitching. Slowly the hour became a day. I still talk to him sometimes. Grief doesn't leave, beti. It moves over and makes room. Go easy. And let people bring you chai.

qa.q: How old was Vandana when her husband died?
qa.a: Twenty-six.

qa.q: Why did Vandana hate being told to be strong?
qa.a: It felt like being asked to hide her grief rather than having it understood.

qa.q: What helped Vandana slowly rebuild her life?
qa.a: Quiet daily company, and going back to her tailoring class one hour at a time until routine and purpose returned.

qa.q: What might it have been like for the girls who kept stitching when Vandana cried?
qa.a: They probably felt for her and chose quiet respect, giving her space without making her feel watched 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls rebuilding routine, support and meaning after the death of her husband, to comfort a grieving young woman.

passage: Six weeks after Sarita's mother died, the Pune office expected her back at full speed, and seven o'clock, when her mother used to call every evening, had become the worst hour of the day. Her phone stayed silent. She stopped cooking; she ate biscuits and stared at the ceiling fan. Her friend Irawati noticed she had stopped replying in the group and turned up on a Thursday with dal and a list. "Not a plan," Irawati said. "Just tiny things." The list said: walk at seven, call Masi on Sundays, cook one real meal a week, see the grief counsellor your office offers. Sarita laughed, then cried. The first walk was ten minutes. The first counselling session was mostly silence. But by the second month, at seven, Sarita was usually out walking, and on Sundays Masi told her stories about her mother as a girl.

qa.q: What time did Sarita's mother use to call?
qa.a: At seven o'clock every evening.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling at seven each evening?
qa.a: Sarita felt a sharp, lonely grief at the hour her mother used to call.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's list of tiny things help more than a big plan?
qa.a: Small steps like a walk at seven and one meal a week were manageable in grief, and the counsellor and Masi added support.

qa.q: How might Masi feel telling stories on Sundays?
qa.a: Masi is probably grieving her sister too, and sharing stories may comfort them both.

grounding: With a friend's help, a grieving young woman rebuilds routine and support after her mother's death while facing work pressure.

passage: The layoff email came at 9:04 on a Monday, and by noon Pallavi's office laptop had been switched off remotely. She sat in her Koramangala PG staring at a black screen. For two weeks she slept till eleven, told her parents in Nagpur she was "working from home", and dodged her friend Samir's calls. On the third Monday Samir turned up with two cutting chais. "You're allowed to be gutted," he said. "You're not allowed to disappear." Together they made a weekday routine: up by eight, two hours of applications, one hour learning something, an evening walk. Pallavi called her parents and told the truth; her father was quiet, then said, "You'll find something. Come home for a week if you want." She began volunteering on Saturday mornings at a coding club for girls from a government school. In the sixth week she got two interviews. She still checked her email with a tight chest.

qa.q: When did the layoff email arrive?
qa.a: At 9:04 on a Monday.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling during the two weeks she slept till eleven?
qa.a: Pallavi felt ashamed and gutted, hiding the layoff from her parents and avoiding calls.

qa.q: What helped Pallavi rebuild after the job loss?
qa.a: A simple weekday routine, telling her parents the truth, and Saturday volunteering that gave her purpose while she searched.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's father have felt hearing the truth?
qa.a: Her father was probably worried but supportive, offering reassurance and a week at home.

grounding: After a sudden layoff in Bengaluru, a young woman rebuilds routine, honesty with family and meaning with a friend's push.

passage:
"The doctor's cleared me to go back to work next month," Sabina said, pulling her shawl tighter on the balcony.
Samir handed her tea. "That's good, na?"
"Is it? Everyone at the office will look at me like I'm made of glass."
"Some will."
"And I don't even know if I want the same job. Eight months of treatment, and I spent them thinking about what mattered. It wasn't quarterly targets."
Samir sat beside her. "What was it?"
"You. Ammi. The women on the ward who shared their food with me." She laughed shakily. "I want to do something for them. The patient support group asked if I'd volunteer."
"Then do both. Go back part-time first. Volunteer on Saturdays."
"And if I get scared again?"
"Then you call me, and I come with samosas, like always."
Sabina leaned her head on his shoulder. "You're a terrible brother."
"The best terrible brother."

qa.q: What has the doctor cleared Sabina to do?
qa.a: Go back to work next month.

qa.q: What was Sabina worried about in returning to the office?
qa.a: Sabina felt anxious that colleagues would treat her as fragile, and unsure whether the old job still mattered.

qa.q: What balance did Samir suggest, and why does it fit?
qa.a: Going back part-time first and volunteering on Saturdays, which rebuilds routine gently while honouring her new sense of meaning.

qa.q: What might Samir be feeling as he sits with his sister?
qa.a: Samir is probably relieved she is recovering, and still protective, promising to come whenever she is scared.

grounding: After months of treatment for a serious illness, a young woman and her brother plan a gentle return to work and new meaning.

passage:
For three months after Papa died, I didn't cook. I lived on biscuits and delivery food and slept at odd hours. The flat felt too quiet and too full of his things at the same time.

It was Ishita who got me started again, but not with advice. She just came every Wednesday evening with vegetables and said, "Chop these with me." We made the dal he used to make. The first time, I cried into the onions and she pretended it was the onions.

After a few weeks, I started buying vegetables myself on Tuesdays, so they'd be ready. Then a morning walk, because Papa used to walk. Then back to my college friends' Sunday call, which I had been avoiding.

I also started seeing a grief counsellor once a week. It helped to say things aloud that I couldn't say to anyone who knew him.

I still miss him terribly. But I'm Parul again, most days, and not only the girl whose father died.

qa.q: What did Ishita bring every Wednesday evening?
qa.a: Ishita came with vegetables and said, "Chop these with me."

qa.q: How was Parul feeling the first time they cooked Papa's dal?
qa.a: Parul was overcome by grief and cried into the onions, missing her father deeply.

qa.q: What small steps helped Parul rebuild her routine?
qa.a: Weekly cooking with Ishita, buying vegetables herself, morning walks, returning to friends' calls and seeing a grief counsellor each helped a little at a time.

qa.q: What was it like for Ishita to cook with Parul during those weeks?
qa.a: Ishita probably felt sad and protective, choosing to stay quietly present and pretend the tears were from the onions to spare Parul embarrassment.

grounding: A young woman looks back on rebuilding routine, support and meaning after her father's death, helped by a friend and a counsellor.

passage:
Support centre note — Santosh, second meeting.

Santosh was laid off from the logistics firm six weeks ago along with forty others. At our first meeting he said he had stopped leaving the house before noon and had not told his parents in Nashik yet. He kept apologising for wasting my time.

Today was different. He had shaved and brought a printed résumé. He said that the night before, he finally called his parents, and his mother said, "Come home for a week, beta." He hasn't decided, but he said the call "took a stone off my chest."

We set a simple routine together: up by eight, two hours of job applications, one hour at the library's free course, a walk in the evening. He also joined the centre's Tuesday group for people who've lost jobs. "At least I won't be the only sad one," he joked.

I noticed his hands were steady today.

— Mohit, career support counsellor

qa.q: How many others were laid off from the logistics firm along with Santosh?
qa.a: Santosh was laid off along with forty others.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after calling his parents?
qa.a: Santosh felt relieved, saying the call "took a stone off my chest", after carrying the secret and the shame of the job loss.

qa.q: How could Mohit keep supporting Santosh's recovery?
qa.a: He could review the daily routine at each meeting, encourage the Tuesday group and help with applications, so Santosh keeps structure and company.

qa.q: How might Santosh's mother have felt when he finally called?
qa.a: She was likely worried and sad for him, but also relieved he told her, which is why she invited him home straight away.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young man rebuilding routine and support after job loss, including telling family and joining a group.

passage:
18 October

Six months since the last treatment. Dr. Pillai says the scans are clear, and everyone keeps saying, "Now you can go back to normal." I don't know what normal is any more.

My body tires at odd times. I used to run the office cricket team. Now I'm happy if I walk to the end of the lane without stopping.

Divyansh has been patient. He doesn't say "normal". Today he just asked, "What do you want your days to look like?" I didn't have an answer, which frightened me.

So tonight I wrote down three things I want back, slowly: my morning walk, painting on Sundays, lunch with my team once a week. Nothing about running the cricket team yet.

I also said yes to the survivors' circle at the hospital. The woman who runs it had the same treatment two years ago. I think I need people who don't need me to explain.

Vinita

qa.q: How long has it been since Vinita's last treatment?
qa.a: It has been six months since the last treatment.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when she had no answer to Divyansh's question?
qa.a: Vinita felt frightened and lost, unsure what daily life should look like after serious illness.

qa.q: What makes Vinita's three-thing list a good way to rebuild?
qa.a: It sets small, slow goals linked to what Vinita values, and joining the survivors' circle adds support from people who understand.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see this time of Vinita's recovery?
qa.a: Divyansh seems patient and caring, perhaps worried, but choosing to ask what Vinita wants rather than pushing for a return to "normal".

grounding: After serious illness, a young adult rebuilds routine, meaning and support in small steps, with Divyansh and a survivors' group.

passage:
Asif's father died in October, suddenly, in their small town near Aligarh. Asif was twenty-five, the eldest son, and suddenly in charge of the family shop, the paperwork and his grieving mother.
For weeks he opened the shop at dawn and closed at night and didn't let himself feel anything. Then one afternoon, a customer asked for "the blue notebooks your father used to keep," and Asif had to go into the back room and sit on a sack of rice until his breathing slowed.
Bhavna, who ran the stationery shop next door, came in with tea. She'd lost her own father two years earlier. "You don't have to be strong every minute," she said.
After that, Asif made small changes. He closed the shop on Friday afternoons to sit with his mother. He asked his cousin to help with the accounts. He began reading his father's old notebooks at night, one page at a time.

qa.q: What did the customer ask Asif for?
qa.a: "The blue notebooks your father used to keep."

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he sat on the sack of rice?
qa.a: Asif was overwhelmed by grief he had been holding back, struggling to breathe calmly.

qa.q: Which of Asif's changes helped him rebuild after the loss?
qa.a: Closing on Friday afternoons for his mother, sharing the accounts and reading his father's notebooks gave him support, rest and a way to grieve.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt bringing Asif tea?
qa.a: Bhavna probably felt compassion and a painful recognition, having lost her own father two years earlier. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a young adult grieving a sudden loss and rebuilding routine, support and meaning.

passage:
Layla was twenty-six and teaching primary school in Beirut when she was diagnosed with a serious illness that meant months of treatment. She had to stop working. Her world shrank to hospital corridors and her flat.
Her friend Tuan, who'd moved there for work, came on Tuesdays. At first Layla didn't want visitors. She felt like a patient, not a person.
One Tuesday he asked, "What do you miss most?" She said, "Being useful. My class."
So they found small ways. She recorded short stories for her pupils on her phone, and their teacher played them in class. On good days she and Tuan walked to the corner bakery. She joined an online group for young adults in treatment and found people who laughed at the same terrible hospital food.
Treatment was still hard. But her days had shape again, and a reason.

qa.q: What did Layla record for her pupils?
qa.a: Short stories on her phone.

qa.q: How did Layla feel at first when Tuan visited?
qa.a: Layla felt low and frustrated, reduced to a patient rather than a person, and didn't want visitors.

qa.q: What helped Layla rebuild meaning during treatment?
qa.a: Finding ways to still be useful, like the stories for her class, plus small outings and an online group of people in similar situations.

qa.q: How might Layla's pupils feel hearing her recorded stories?
qa.a: The pupils probably feel happy and connected to their teacher, even while she's away.

grounding: Shows a young adult facing serious illness and rebuilding routine, support and meaning.

passage: The grief support group met in a borrowed classroom at the community centre, plastic chairs in a circle. Asif had come three times and said nothing. His father had died in March, and in May the logistics firm let him go in a round of cuts. Most days he woke at noon and scrolled until dark. Tonight Irawati, the facilitator, asked each person for one small thing that had helped that week. When it reached Asif, his throat closed. Then he said, "I made chai at six this morning, the way my father used to. I drank it on the balcony. That's all." Nobody rushed him. "That's not all," Irawati said gently. "That's a routine starting." After the session an older man handed Asif a card for a job-search group that met on Tuesdays. Asif put it in his wallet, next to his father's photo.

qa.q: Where did the grief support group meet?
qa.a: In a borrowed classroom at the community centre.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when it was his turn to speak?
qa.a: He felt grief so heavy that his throat closed, along with a small, shaky hope as he shared the morning chai.

qa.q: How did the group support Asif's recovery?
qa.a: They gave him time without rushing, Irawati named the chai as a routine starting, and a member pointed him to a job-search group.

qa.q: How might Irawati see Asif speaking for the first time?
qa.a: She likely sees it as an important step after three silent sessions and wants him to recognise it as progress.

grounding: Shows a young adult beginning to rebuild routine and support after bereavement and job loss.
